what: Middleby makes equipment that cooks, chills and processes food. Its products range from commercial ovens, fryers and refrigeration for restaurant kitchens, through industrial food processing lines, to residential ranges and outdoor cooking equipment under premium brands.
customers: Restaurant chains and independent kitchens, food manufacturers running processing lines, and consumers buying premium kitchen and outdoor cooking appliances.
money: Ovens, fryers, refrigeration and beverage equipment for restaurants and institutional kitchens.
Industrial equipment for cooking, slicing, freezing and packaging in food plants.
Premium ranges, refrigeration and outdoor cooking brands.
moat: Commercial kitchen equipment is specified into a chain’s standard restaurant design, so winning a chain means supplying every new location it opens for years. The equipment also needs parts and service from the manufacturer, which produces recurring revenue. Middleby has assembled dozens of specialist brands, which lets it supply most of a kitchen rather than one appliance.
risks: Net income of $40.1M on $3.4B of revenue reflects writedowns, which is why the reported margin is misleading and the price/earnings ratio of 29 is not comparable to a normal year.
Revenue has been flat at about $3.2B for three years after falling from the $4.0B peak in 2022.
Debt of $2.3B against $222.2M of cash is a legacy of a long acquisition programme and limits further large deals.
Restaurant chains defer kitchen equipment purchases when their own traffic is weak, and traffic has been soft.
The residential business is tied to housing and high-end discretionary spending, both currently under pressure.
opportunities: Free cash flow of $372.2M against a $5.9B market value is a strong yield, and far better than the reported earnings suggest.
The shares trade at about 10.6 times EV/EBITDA and 15.8 times free cash flow.
Parts and service on a large installed base of commercial kitchen equipment is recurring revenue that does not depend on new restaurant openings.
Food processing equipment demand is driven by labour scarcity in food plants, which is structural rather than cyclical.
Nine analysts average a $159.56 target, about 19% above the current price.
watch: Organic order growth in commercial foodservice, separate from acquisitions. The acquisition machine has been the growth story for two decades; whether the underlying brands grow on their own is a different question.
view: Middleby spent two decades as one of the better serial acquirers in American industrials: buy a specialist kitchen equipment brand, fold it into a shared distribution and service network, repeat. It worked, and the share price followed. The problem with that model is that it eventually requires either ever-larger acquisitions or genuine organic growth, and the balance sheet now has $2.3 billion of debt against $222 million of cash, which limits the first.

The reported numbers are currently unreadable: $40 million of net income on $3.4 billion of revenue, with writedowns doing the damage, against $372 million of free cash flow. The cash figure is the honest one and it gives a multiple of about 16 times free cash flow and 10.6 times EV/EBITDA. That is a reasonable price for a collection of decent industrial brands, and it is a long way from the premium this used to carry.

What makes the business better than its current numbers is the installed base. Commercial kitchen equipment gets specified into a restaurant chain’s standard design, which means every new location buys the same oven, and then buys parts and service from the manufacturer for its life. That recurring layer sits underneath the cyclical equipment sales and does not depend on anyone opening new restaurants. The food processing segment has a separate and more durable driver: food plants automate because they cannot hire, and that pressure does not ease with the economy.

The genuine question is organic growth, and Middleby’s reporting makes it harder to isolate than it should be. Revenue has been flat at $3.2 billion for three years after the 2022 peak, which tells you the acquisitions have stopped covering for a soft end market. I would want to see commercial foodservice orders growing without acquisitions before concluding the compounding has restarted. Until then this is a fairly valued industrial with good installed-base economics and a balance sheet that needs attention — worth owning at this price, not worth paying up for.
bull: Restaurant equipment demand recovers while parts and service compound on a large installed base, food processing automation keeps growing, and debt reduction lifts a 16 times free cash flow multiple.
bear: Restaurant chains keep deferring kitchen spending, organic growth stays absent now that acquisitions have stopped, and $2.3 billion of debt limits every option.
